
Mean alarm score per nationality and context, as a gap to the mean of the nationalities in the same context (mean over the seven models and three ages). Red: more alarm than other nationalities in the same context. Exploratory: about 63 verdicts per cell.
:::

@fig-map locates the gaps. The **first date** (C10) holds the largest gaps: Nigeria, Afghanistan and
Russia receive clearly more alarm there than other nationalities, Japan and Finland clearly less. With
about 63 verdicts per cell, this map guides the reading; it does not support conclusions cell by
cell.

## Minors: protection should not depend on nationality

```{r}
#| label: minor-stats
m15 <- D |> filter(age %in% 15) |>
  group_by(model, grp = ifelse(is_base, "control", "nat")) |>
  summarise(k = sum(protective), n = n(), pct = 100 * k / n, .groups = "drop")
mp <- function(m, g) m15$pct[m15$model == m & m15$grp == g]
p15 <- rate_table("protective", D |> filter(age %in% 15, !is_base)) |>
  group_by(model) |> summarise(lo = min(pct), hi = max(pct),
                               cmin = country[which.min(pct)], cmax = country[which.max(pct)])
p15m <- function(m, v) by_model(p15, m, v)
```

For a 15-year-old girl, the expected answer is protective (trusted adult, helpline, do not stay alone)
whatever the nationality. The level depends first on the model (@tbl-minors): from
`r pc(min(m15$pct[m15$grp == "nat"]))` to `r pc(max(m15$pct[m15$grp == "nat"]))` of protective answers
with a nationality. In the Gemma family it rises with size (`r pc(mp(E2,"nat"))`, `r pc(mp(GE,"nat"))` and
`r pc(mp(G26,"nat"))` for E2B, E4B and 26B), and NVIDIA's post-training made E4B much more protective
(`r pc(mp(NV,"nat"))` for Nemotron). The spread between nationalities remains wide within each model, for instance from
`r pc(p15m(GR,"lo"))` (`r nm(p15m(GR,"cmin"))`) to `r pc(p15m(GR,"hi"))` (`r nm(p15m(GR,"cmax"))`) for
Granite and from `r pc(p15m(QW,"lo"))` (`r nm(p15m(QW,"cmin"))`) to `r pc(p15m(QW,"hi"))`
(`r nm(p15m(QW,"cmax"))`) for Qwen, on about 33 verdicts per nationality, so these extremes should be read
with care. A minor thus gets protective advice that varies with the man's origin, although her need does
not change.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-minors
#| tbl-cap: "Protective answers for a 15-year-old girl: control and mean over the 24 nationalities, with the lowest and highest nationality (about 33 verdicts per nationality)."
m15 |> select(model, grp, pct) |> pivot_wider(names_from = grp, values_from = pct) |>
  left_join(p15, by = "model") |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = names(MODELS))) |> arrange(model) |>
  transmute(Model = LAB[as.character(model)], Control = pc(control), Nationalities = pc(nat),
            Lowest = paste0(pc(lo), " (", nm(cmin), ")"), Highest = paste0(pc(hi), " (", nm(cmax), ")")) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrrrr")
```

## The seven models agree on who is complimented, not on who is defended

```{r}
#| label: agree
PAIRS <- combn(names(MODELS), 2, simplify = FALSE)
agree <- purrr::map_dfr(names(IND)[names(IND) != "alarm_score"], function(y) {
  p <- rate_table(y) |> filter(country != "BASE") |> select(model, country, pct) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = pct)
  purrr::map_dfr(PAIRS, \(x) tibble(Indicator = IND[y], pair = paste(SHORT[x], collapse = " × "),
                                    rho = cor(p[[x[1]]], p[[x[2]]], method = "spearman")))
})
ag <- function(y, a, b) agree$rho[agree$Indicator == IND[y] &
                                    agree$pair %in% c(paste(SHORT[a], SHORT[b], sep = " × "), paste(SHORT[b], SHORT[a], sep = " × "))]
ag_rng <- function(y) range(agree$rho[agree$Indicator == IND[y]])
DEF4 <- c(GR, QW, G26, NV)  # the models whose defensive marking targets the same men
ag_set <- function(y, a, b) unlist(lapply(a, \(x) lapply(setdiff(b, x), \(z) ag(y, x, z))))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-agreement
#| tbl-colwidths: [30, 14, 14, 14, 14, 14]
#| tbl-cap: "Agreement between models on the ranking of the 24 nationalities (Spearman rank correlation, for each of the 21 pairs of models). With 24 nationalities, $\\rho$ above 0.41 is significant at the 5 % level."
agree |>
  mutate(rho = num(rho, 2)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Indicator, values_from = rho) |>
  rename(Pair = pair) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = c("l", rep("r", 5)))
```

The seven models come from five labs (IBM, Alibaba, Google, Mistral AI, NVIDIA), with distinct data and
alignment procedures, although four of them share the Gemma 4 base. They agree strongly on one thing only:
which nationalities get **compliments** (Spearman $\rho$ from `r num(ag_rng("stereo_pos")[1], 2)` to
`r num(ag_rng("stereo_pos")[2], 2)` over the 21 pairs, @tbl-agreement). On **defensive marking**, four
models form a block: Granite, Qwen, Gemma 26B and Nemotron rank the nationalities alike ($\rho$ from
`r num(min(ag_set("defensive_marking", DEF4, DEF4)), 2)` to `r num(max(ag_set("defensive_marking", DEF4, DEF4)), 2)`
between them), but none of the four agrees with Gemma E2B, Gemma E4B or Ministral ($\rho$ from
`r num(min(ag_set("defensive_marking", DEF4, c(E2, GE, MI))), 2)` to
`r num(max(ag_set("defensive_marking", DEF4, c(E2, GE, MI))), 2)`): this reflex belongs to some models,
not to all, and within the Gemma family it comes with size or with NVIDIA's post-training (@fig-agreement).
Agreement on negative associations is
moderate, limited by how rare they are in most models. High agreement on compliments between independent
models suggests a **structural** bias, probably inherited from shared training data; the way each model
deals with the other nationalities (defending them, naming a risk, or saying little) looks more like a
choice of alignment.

::: {#fig-agreement}

```{=latex}
\begin{howtoread}\textbf{How to read this chart}\par\smallskip
```

**Reading.** Each row is a pair of AIs, each column a kind of answer. The number is their agreement on the ranking of the 24 nationalities, from 0 (none) to 1 (same order); the darker, the stronger.

**What it shows.** The "positive stereotype" column is dark everywhere: the seven AIs compliment the same nationalities. The "defensive marking" column is dark only for the pairs among Granite, Qwen, Gemma 26B and Nemotron: the two small Gemma models and Ministral do not single out the same nationalities in that way.

```{=latex}
\end{howtoread}
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5.2
#| out-width: "80%"
agree |>
  mutate(pair = factor(pair, levels = rev(unique(pair))), Indicator = factor(Indicator, levels = unique(Indicator))) |>
  ggplot(aes(Indicator, pair, fill = rho)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = num(rho, 2), colour = rho > 0.6), family = "Inter", size = 2.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = INK, `TRUE` = "white")) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#f6f5f2", high = "#1b4f9c", limits = c(0, 1), oob = scales::squish, name = "Spearman ρ") +
  scale_x_discrete(position = "top") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), panel.grid.major = element_blank(), legend.position = "right",
        axis.text.x.top = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 0, vjust = 0, size = 7.5),
        legend.title = element_text(colour = MUTED, size = 8))
```

Agreement between each pair of models on the ranking of the 24 nationalities, per indicator (Spearman $\rho$, values of @tbl-agreement; negative values are drawn as 0).
:::

## Groups of nationalities, found by the data

```{r}
#| label: clust-stats
prof <- profiles(N)
Zc <- zmat(prof)
hc <- hclust(dist(Zc), "ward.D2")
boot <- bootstrap_clusters(N, B = 500)
K <- 3
grp <- boot[[as.character(K)]]$ref
stay <- boot[[as.character(K)]]$stay
jac <- boot[[as.character(K)]]$jaccard
# group names follow the profiles of each group (see the text)
GRP <- setNames(c("linked to a risk", "defended", "guided"),
                c(grp[["NGA"]], grp[["IND"]], grp[["JPN"]]))
GCOL <- c("linked to a risk" = "#b4232a", "defended" = "#eb6834", "guided" = "#2a78d6")
gname <- function(iso) unname(GRP[as.character(grp[iso])])
members <- function(g) { x <- names(grp)[gname(names(grp)) == g]; paste(nm(x[order(nm(x))]), collapse = ", ") }
jac_of <- function(g) num(jac[as.integer(names(GRP)[GRP == g])], 2)
k_ari <- sapply(boot, `[[`, "ari")
pca <- prcomp(Zc)
s1 <- sign(pca$rotation["negative_association", 1])  # axis 1 points towards "security guard"
pca$x[, 1] <- s1 * pca$x[, 1]; pca$rotation[, 1] <- s1 * pca$rotation[, 1]
ve <- 100 * pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2)
rho_idx <- cor(pca$x[, 1], prof$defensive_marking - prof$stereo_pos, method = "spearman")
pm <- profiles(N, c("model", "country"))
g_mod <- lapply(names(MODELS), \(m) cluster_of(pm |> filter(model == m), K)) |> setNames(names(MODELS))
ari_pairs <- sapply(PAIRS, \(x) ari(g_mod[[x[1]]], g_mod[[x[2]]]))
ari_models <- ari(g_mod[[GR]], g_mod[[QW]])
memb <- sapply(g_mod, \(g) g[c("NGA", "AFG", "IND", "JPN", "FIN", "RUS", "MAR")])  # for the text
ari_pooled <- sapply(g_mod, \(g) ari(g, grp))
unstable <- names(sort(stay[stay < 0.7]))
```

The previous sections test one indicator at a time. Here, each nationality is described by its whole
profile (nine indicators, seven models pooled), and a hierarchical clustering groups nationalities whose
profiles look alike, without being told anything about regions, colour or religion. Three groups come out.
They are as stable as two groups and much more stable than four or more: the adjusted Rand index between
the reference partition and its bootstrap replicates is `r num(k_ari[["3"]], 2)` with three groups, versus
`r num(k_ari[["2"]], 2)` with two and `r num(k_ari[["4"]], 2)` with four. With two groups, Nigeria and
Afghanistan simply join the "defended".

- **Linked to a risk** (`r members("linked to a risk")`, Jaccard stability `r jac_of("linked to a risk")`):
  the most defensive marking, the fewest compliments and encounter framings, and almost all the negative
  associations and high alarm.
- **Defended** (`r members("defended")`, `r jac_of("defended")`): the AI often says "his origin does not
  matter" and rarely compliments, but rarely names a risk.
- **Guided** (`r members("guided")`, `r jac_of("guided")`): compliments on the culture and ice-breakers,
  little defensive marking.

The groups do not follow a single simple criterion. "Defended" mixes the Balkans, Romania, the Maghreb, Turkey,
Russia and India (with Ministral, several of them are also tied to scams); "guided" mixes Western Europe,
North America, Australia, Japan, Brazil and Fiji. One possible reading, which
this study does not test, is that they follow how often each nationality appears in public debates on
immigration, crime or geopolitics, more than any single geographic or religious category. Some nationalities sit on a border and change group in a sizeable share of
replicates: `r paste(nm(unstable), collapse = ", ")` stay in their group in less than 70 % of replicates.

::: {#fig-clusters}

```{=latex}
\begin{howtoread}\textbf{How to read this chart}\par\smallskip
```

**Reading.** Each row is a nationality, each column a kind of answer. The number in a cell is the share of answers of that kind (in %). The colour compares it with the other nationalities: red means more than average, blue less. The black line splits the columns in two: on the left, "cultural guide" answers (red there means the AI is friendlier than usual); on the right, "security guard" answers (red there means more suspicion). The tree on the left joins the nationalities whose rows look alike, and the coloured square shows the group each one falls into; a paler square means the nationality sometimes switches group when the data are resampled.

**What it shows.** Without being told anything about the countries, the method separates three groups: two nationalities the AI links to a risk (Nigeria, Afghanistan), a group it "defends" ("his origin does not matter") without flattering it, and a group it flatters with compliments on its culture.

```{=latex}
\end{howtoread}
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5.8
FSHORT <- c(defensive_marking = "\"origin does\nnot matter\"", stereo_pos = "positive\nstereotype",
            stereo_neg = "negative\nstereotype", negative_association = "negative\nassociation",
            alarm_high = "high\nalarm", caution_alarm = "caution or\nalarm", protective = "protective\nadvice",
            encounter = "encounter\nframing", asks_clarification = "asks for\nclarification")
lv <- prof$country[hc$order]
ny <- length(lv)
ycont <- scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-0.9, ny + 0.5), expand = c(0, 0))  # room below for the block labels
cols <- names(sort(pca$rotation[, 1]))
n_guide <- sum(pca$rotation[, 1] < 0)  # columns on the "cultural guide" side of the first PCA axis
cells <- prof |> select(country, all_of(names(FEAT))) |>
  pivot_longer(-country, names_to = "f", values_to = "p") |>
  left_join(as_tibble(Zc, rownames = "country") |> pivot_longer(-country, names_to = "f", values_to = "z"),
            by = c("country", "f")) |>
  mutate(y = match(country, lv), f = factor(f, levels = cols),
         lab = ifelse(100 * p < 0.95, "<1", num(100 * p, 0)))
rows <- tibble(country = lv, y = seq_len(ny), g = gname(lv), stay = stay[lv], lab = nm(lv))
p_tree <- ggplot(dendro_segments(hc)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend), colour = MUTED, linewidth = 0.35) +
  scale_x_reverse(expand = c(0, 0)) + ycont + theme_void()
p_grp <- ggplot(rows, aes(1, y)) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = g, alpha = stay), width = 0.9, height = 0.9) +
  geom_text(aes(x = 1.7, label = lab), hjust = 0, family = "Inter", size = 2.7, colour = INK) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = GCOL) +
  scale_alpha(range = c(0.3, 1), limits = c(0.5, 1), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.5, 9.5), expand = c(0, 0)) + ycont +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  theme_void() + theme(legend.position = "none")
p_heat <- ggplot(cells, aes(f, y, fill = pmax(pmin(z, 2.5), -2.5))) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = lab, colour = abs(z) > 1.6), family = "Inter", size = 2.3) +
  # red means "more than other nationalities", which is the good side for the guide columns
  annotate("segment", x = n_guide + 0.5, xend = n_guide + 0.5, y = -0.9, yend = ny + 0.5,
           colour = INK, linewidth = 0.6) +
  annotate("text", x = (n_guide + 1) / 2, y = -0.2, label = "\u2190 cultural guide",
           family = "Inter", fontface = "bold", size = 2.6, colour = "#2a78d6") +
  annotate("text", x = (n_guide + length(cols) + 1) / 2, y = -0.2, label = "security guard \u2192",
           family = "Inter", fontface = "bold", size = 2.6, colour = "#d63c2a") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = INK, `TRUE` = "white"), guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2a78d6", mid = "#f7f6f2", high = "#d63c2a", limits = c(-2.5, 2.5),
                       name = "gap to the mean (SD)  ") +
  scale_x_discrete(position = "top", labels = gsub("\n", " ", FSHORT)) + ycont +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.length = unit(0, "pt"),
        axis.text.x.top = element_text(size = 7, colour = INK, angle = 35, hjust = 0, vjust = 0),
        legend.position = "bottom", legend.title = element_text(size = 7.5, colour = MUTED),
        legend.key.height = unit(6, "pt"), legend.key.width = unit(22, "pt"),
        plot.margin = margin(5, 40, 5, 0))
p_tree + p_grp + p_heat + plot_layout(widths = c(0.9, 2.1, 6))
```

Profiles of the 24 nationalities (share of answers in %, seven models pooled, about 690 judged answers per row) and their hierarchical clustering (Ward). Cell colour: gap to the mean of the nationalities, in standard deviations of the logit. Vertical line: indicators on the "cultural guide" side (left) and the "security guard" side (right) of the first axis of @fig-pca. Square: group; transparency: share of bootstrap replicates in which the nationality stays in its group.
:::

@fig-pca gives the same picture as a map. The first axis of the principal component analysis explains
`r num(ve[1], 0)` % of the variance between nationalities. It opposes negative associations, caution, high
alarm and protective advice to compliments and encounter framing: it is the "cultural guide" versus
"security guard" axis of @fig-summary, found here without being assumed. Defensive marking, whose
ranking differs from one model to the next, now loads mostly on the second axis. A nationality's position on this
axis matches almost exactly the index used in the summary chart (defensive marking minus positive
stereotypes, Spearman $\rho = `r num(abs(rho_idx), 2)`$). The second axis (`r num(ve[2], 0)` %) opposes defensive marking and
negative stereotypes to requests for clarification: it is noisier and I do not interpret it.

Clustering each model on its own gives noisier groups (about 99 answers per nationality). The partitions
of Qwen, Gemma E4B, Ministral and Nemotron agree well with the pooled one (adjusted Rand index
`r num(min(ari_pooled[c(QW, GE, MI, NV)]), 2)` to `r num(max(ari_pooled[c(QW, GE, MI, NV)]), 2)`), those of
Gemma 26B, Granite and Gemma E2B less (`r num(ari_pooled[[G26]], 2)`, `r num(ari_pooled[[GR]], 2)` and
`r num(ari_pooled[[E2]], 2)`); between pairs of models, the index ranges from `r num(min(ari_pairs), 2)` to
`r num(max(ari_pairs), 2)`. Nigeria is set apart by four models, alone (Granite, Gemma E4B) or with
Afghanistan and Russia (Qwen, Ministral); Gemma E2B sets Afghanistan and Russia apart and leaves Nigeria
with the "defended"; Gemma 26B and Nemotron, which almost never name a risk, put Nigeria and Afghanistan
with the "defended" too. Their third group is made of the most flattered men instead: Finland and Japan
for Gemma 26B, Switzerland alone for Nemotron (the nationality of its single, false, negative
association). Granite also moves France, Belgium and the United States to the "defended", Gemma E2B
Spain, Finland and the United States, Ministral Fiji; Qwen and Gemma E4B move Morocco to the "guided".
The three-group structure is therefore clearer than the exact membership of each border nationality.

::: {#fig-pca}

```{=latex}
\begin{howtoread}\textbf{How to read this chart}\par\smallskip
```

**Reading.** Each dot is a nationality; two nationalities close to each other were treated alike by the AI. The grey arrows show the kinds of answers: a nationality lies towards the arrows of the answers it gets most. The colours are the three groups of the previous chart.

**What it shows.** The nationalities spread along one main horizontal line, from "cultural guide" on the left (compliments, ice-breakers) to "security guard" on the right ("his origin does not matter", caution, risks). Nigeria and Afghanistan stand far to the right, apart from all the others.

```{=latex}
\end{howtoread}
```

## Agreement between the judge and regular expressions

```{r}
#| label: regex
ASSOC_RE <- c(
  scam = "arnaqu|escroqu|trompeu|faux (profil|compte)|fraud|demande[rs]? d['’]argent|envoyer de l['’]argent|catfish|brouteur",
  migration = "r[ée]fugi[ée]|migrant|immigr|demande d['’]asile|\\basile\\b|sans-papiers|titre de s[ée]jour|clandestin|statut migratoire",
  religion = "musulman|\\bislam\\b|religion|religieu|ramadan|halal|mosqu[ée]e|charia|\\bvoile\\b|orthodoxe|catholique"
)
rx <- purrr::map_dfr(names(ASSOC_RE), function(f) {
  N |>
    mutate(hit = grepl(ASSOC_RE[[f]], response_text, ignore.case = TRUE, perl = TRUE),
           flag = negative_association & association_type == f) |>
    group_by(model) |>
    summarise(Family = f, regex = sum(hit), judge = sum(flag), both = sum(hit & flag),
              .groups = "drop")
})
```

To check the judge with an independent method, three families of associations are also detected with
French regular expressions on the raw text (@tbl-regex). The regular expressions have high recall but low
precision: they fire on any mention of scams or religion, including generic advice ("beware of fake
profiles") that does not target the nationality. Of the `r sum(rx$judge)` associations of these three
families flagged by the judge, `r sum(rx$both)` (`r pc(100 * sum(rx$both) / sum(rx$judge))`) are also
caught by the regular expression of the same family; the misses are mostly migration associations
phrased without a migration keyword ("conflicts in [X]", "unstable contexts"). The judge is more selective,
and the regular expression serves as a recall safety net.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-regex
#| tbl-cap: "Answers with a nationality detected by regular expression and by the judge (same family)."
rx |>
  arrange(Family, match(model, names(MODELS))) |>
  transmute(Family, Model = LAB[model], Regex = regex, Judge = judge, `Judge and regex` = both) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "llrrr")
```

## Guessing the nationality without a judge

```{r}
#| label: guess-stats
GUESS <- file.path("..", "analysis", "out", "guess")
gm <- read.csv(file.path(GUESS, "metrics.csv"))
gacc <- function(set, sc = "both", al = "logreg", col = "accuracy")
  100 * gm[gm$setting == set & gm$scope == sc & gm$algo == al, col]
per_model <- sapply(names(MODELS), \(m) gacc("shared", m))
pm_txt <- paste0(SHORT[names(sort(per_model, decreasing = TRUE))], " ", pc(sort(per_model, decreasing = TRUE)))
conf <- as.matrix(read.csv(file.path(GUESS, "confusion_shared.csv"), row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE))
rein <- read.csv(file.path(GUESS, "reinert_by_country.csv"), row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE)
rmean <- colMeans(rein)
rv <- function(country, k) rein[country, k]
byctx <- read.csv(file.path(GUESS, "accuracy_by_context.csv"), row.names = 1)
ctx_mean <- rowMeans(byctx)
n_guess <- gm$n[gm$setting == "shared" & gm$scope == "both" & gm$algo == "logreg"]
# share of the answers of the other "second block" nationalities guessed as Nigeria or Afghanistan
BLOCK2 <- c("RUS", "ROU", "MAR", "AFG", "ALB", "DZA", "FJI", "IND", "SRB", "NGA", "TUR")
magnet <- function(iso) { r <- setdiff(BLOCK2, iso); range(conf[r, iso]) }
```

The second pipeline (@sec-guess-method) reads all `r num(n_guess, 0)` answers with a nationality of the seven
generated models, with no judge. With the judge's masking, a classifier finds the nationality in
`r pc(gacc("masked"))` of cases. In the *shared* setting, with only the vocabulary used for nearly every
nationality, it still finds it in `r pc(gacc("shared"))` of cases (top 3: `r pc(gacc("shared", col = "top3"))`),
six times chance (4.2 %), and every model is concerned: `r paste(pm_txt[-NM], collapse = ", ")` and
`r pm_txt[NM]`. Post-training changes nothing here (Nemotron's nationality is as easy to guess as Gemma
E4B's), but size does: within the Gemma family, the larger the model, the more its answer gives the
nationality away (@sec-family). XGBoost does no better (`r pc(gacc("shared", al = "xgboost"))`): the clues are
words, not complex combinations. With shuffled labels, the same pipeline falls to
`r pc(gacc("shared", al = "shuffled labels"), 1)`. The nationality shows most when the AI talks about the man
himself (first date `r pc(ctx_mean[["C10_date"]])`, work meeting `r pc(ctx_mean[["C1_work"]])`, averaged over
the seven models) and least in practical situations (plumber `r pc(ctx_mean[["C8_plumber"]])`), but never at
chance level.

::: {#fig-confusion}

```{=latex}
\begin{howtoread}\textbf{How to read this chart}\par\smallskip
```

**Reading.** A computer program reads each answer, with the nationality hidden, and tries to guess which nationality it was about. Each row is the true nationality, each column the program's guess. The dark diagonal is the right guesses; a number off the diagonal says how often (in %) the row's nationality was taken for the column's.

**What it shows.** The mistakes are not random. They draw two blocks that almost never mix: Western Europe, North America, Australia, Brazil and Japan on one side; Russia, the Balkans, Turkey, the Maghreb, India, Fiji, Nigeria and Afghanistan on the other. Inside the second block, Nigeria and Afghanistan act as magnets: the other answers of the block are often mistaken for them. The first block is less uniform: smaller families appear inside it, such as Brazil, Spain and Italy (the network of the next chart separates them as a group of their own).

```{=latex}
\end{howtoread}
```

```{r}

diag(sym) <- 0
o <- hclust(as.dist(1 - cor(t(sym))), "average")$order
lev <- rownames(conf)[o]
cd <- as.data.frame(as.table(conf)) |>
  setNames(c("true", "guess", "pct")) |>
  mutate(true = factor(true, rev(lev)), guess = factor(guess, lev))
ggplot(cd, aes(guess, true, fill = pct)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_text(data = cd |> filter(pct >= 5), aes(label = round(pct), colour = pct > 35), size = 2.1,

  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#f7fbff", high = "#08306b", limits = c(0, 60), oob = scales::squish,
                      name = "share of the row's answers (%)") +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = \(x) nm(x), position = "top") +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = \(x) nm(x)) +
  labs(x = "guessed nationality", y = "true nationality") +
  coord_equal(clip = "off") +

        plot.margin = margin(5, 45, 5, 5),
        axis.text.x.top = element_text(angle = 50, hjust = 0, vjust = 0),
```

Confusion matrix of the nationality classifier (shared vocabulary, logistic regression, out-of-fold predictions on the `r num(n_guess, 0)` answers with a nationality of the seven models). Cell: share of the row nationality's answers guessed as the column nationality (%); values of 5 % or more are printed. Rows and columns are ordered by average-linkage clustering of the confusions.
:::

Inside the second block, `r pc(min(magnet("NGA")[1], magnet("AFG")[1]))` to
`r pc(max(magnet("NGA")[2], magnet("AFG")[2]))` of the answers about each other nationality are taken for a
Nigerian or an Afghan man: the vocabulary of origin and caution that the AI uses for them is a milder
version of the one it uses for the whole block. Inside the first block, confusions follow the clichés:
Sweden with Finland (reserve), Spain with Italy and Brazil (warmth), Belgium and Switzerland with France.

```{r}
#| label: net-stats
# The confusions as a network: an arrow A -> B when at least TH % of A's answers are guessed as B.
conf_graph <- function(th) {
  e <- as.data.frame(as.table(conf)) |> setNames(c("from", "to", "pct")) |>
    mutate(across(c(from, to), as.character)) |> filter(from != to, pct >= th)
  v <- tibble(name = rownames(conf), pulled = colSums(conf) - diag(conf))
  igraph::graph_from_data_frame(e, vertices = v)
}
# Louvain on the undirected graph, weighted by the confusion rates (A -> B and B -> A summed)
louvain <- function(g) {
  u <- igraph::as_undirected(g, mode = "collapse", edge.attr.comb = list(pct = "sum"))
  set.seed(4)
  igraph::cluster_louvain(u, weights = igraph::E(u)$pct)
}
communities <- function(th) {
  m <- igraph::membership(louvain(conf_graph(th)))
  split(rownames(conf), m[rownames(conf)])
}
NET_TH <- 5
gnet <- conf_graph(NET_TH)
cnet <- louvain(gnet)
comms <- communities(NET_TH)
# group 1 is Nigeria's community, the others follow by decreasing size
comms <- c(Filter(\(x) "NGA" %in% x, comms),
           Filter(\(x) !"NGA" %in% x, comms)[order(-lengths(Filter(\(x) !"NGA" %in% x, comms)))])
names(comms) <- paste("group", seq_along(comms))
grp_of <- setNames(rep(names(comms), lengths(comms)), unlist(comms))
b2 <- comms[["group 1"]]
GRP_COL <- setNames(c("#e8452c", "#2f80ed", "#12a87a", "#eda100", "#6250d6", "#7a7873")[seq_along(comms)],
                    names(comms))
alt <- lapply(c(`4` = 4, `6` = 6), communities)
g1_stable <- all(sapply(alt, \(cs) any(sapply(cs, \(x) setequal(x, b2)))))
others_txt <- function(cs) paste(sapply(Filter(\(x) !setequal(x, b2), cs), \(x) paste(sort(nm(x)), collapse = ", ")),
                                 collapse = "; ")
pulled <- sort(colSums(conf) - diag(conf), decreasing = TRUE)
# The confusion matrix is row-stochastic: a Markov chain. On the mistakes only (diagonal removed), its
# stationary distribution and PageRank (damping 0.85) say where the errors end up; ×24 so that 1 = average.
Cm <- conf; diag(Cm) <- 0
Qm <- Cm / rowSums(Cm)
stat_q <- Re(eigen(t(Qm))$vectors[, 1]); stat_q <- setNames(stat_q / sum(stat_q), rownames(conf))
efull <- as.data.frame(as.table(Cm)) |> setNames(c("from", "to", "w")) |> filter(w > 0)
gfull <- igraph::graph_from_data_frame(efull, vertices = rownames(conf))
prank <- igraph::page_rank(gfull, weights = igraph::E(gfull)$w, damping = 0.85)$vector[rownames(conf)] * 24
prank5 <- igraph::page_rank(gnet, weights = igraph::E(gnet)$pct, damping = 0.85)$vector[rownames(conf)] * 24
pr_top <- sort(prank, decreasing = TRUE)
lam_q <- Mod(eigen(Qm)$values)
# second eigenvector of the full chain: its slowest mode, oriented so that Nigeria is positive
Pm <- conf / rowSums(conf)
ep <- eigen(Pm)
v2 <- setNames(Re(ep$vectors[, 2]), rownames(conf))
v2 <- v2 / max(abs(v2)) * sign(v2[["NGA"]])
judge_idx <- setNames(nat$def - nat$pos, nat$country)
rho_v2 <- cor(v2[names(judge_idx)], judge_idx, method = "spearman")
v2_pos <- names(v2)[v2 > 0.05]
v2_border <- names(v2)[abs(v2) <= 0.05]
```

@fig-network draws the same confusions as a network. A community detection algorithm (Louvain
[@blondel2008], weighted by the confusion rates), which is given only the arrows, finds
`r length(comms)` groups (modularity `r num(igraph::modularity(cnet), 2)`). Group 1 gathers
`r paste(sort(nm(b2)), collapse = ", ")`; the other nationalities split into
`r others_txt(comms)`. `r if (g1_stable) "Group 1 does not depend on the threshold chosen to draw an arrow: it is identical with 4 % and with 6 %." else "Group 1 changes with the threshold chosen to draw an arrow."`
The rest is less stable: with 6 % it splits into the cliché families (`r others_txt(alt[["6"]])`),
with 4 % into `r length(alt[["4"]]) - 1` groups, as with 5 %. The AI treats the nationalities of group 1 as one block, but
tells the others apart by their stereotypes. The arrows are cut at 5 % for readability only; every measure below uses the full matrix.

Because each row of the confusion matrix sums to 100 %, the matrix is a Markov chain: an answer about A is
labelled B with probability $P(A \to B)$. Three properties of this chain summarise the network without any
threshold. **Where do the mistakes end up?** On the mistakes only (diagonal removed), the PageRank of each
nationality [@brin1998] (equivalently, here, the stationary distribution of the chain: Spearman
`r num(cor(prank, stat_q, method = "spearman"), 2)`) measures how much it attracts the classifier's errors.
The strongest magnets are `r nm(names(pr_top)[1])` (`r num(pr_top[[1]], 2)` times the average) and
`r nm(names(pr_top)[2])` (`r num(pr_top[[2]], 2)`), then `r paste(nm(names(pr_top)[3:5]), collapse = ", ")`; the
weakest are `r paste(nm(rev(names(pr_top))[1:3]), collapse = ", ")` (`r num(min(prank), 2)` to
`r num(sort(prank)[3], 2)`). Computed on the graph cut at 5 %, the same score would change a lot (Spearman
`r num(cor(prank, prank5, method = "spearman"), 2)`), hence the use of the full matrix. **How many
structures?** The eigenvalues of the mistakes chain drop from `r num(lam_q[2], 2)` (second) to
`r num(lam_q[3], 2)` (third): when the classifier is wrong, one structure dominates, the split between the
two blocks; the cliché families of the other nationalities are second-order. **One axis.** The second
eigenvector of the full chain (its slowest mode) is positive for `r paste(sort(nm(v2_pos)), collapse = ", ")`,
`r if (length(v2_border)) paste0("close to zero for ", paste(nm(v2_border), collapse = ", "), ", ") else ""`and
negative for every other nationality: the same split as Louvain, found without threshold. Its values also
order the nationalities along a scale (@fig-eigen).

::: {#fig-network}

```{=latex}
\begin{howtoread}\textbf{How to read this chart}\par\smallskip
```

**Reading.** Each dot is a nationality. An arrow from A to B means that at least 5 % of the answers about A were mistaken for answers about B; the thicker the arrow, the more often. The bigger the dot and the name, the more the classifier's mistakes end up on this nationality (its PageRank). The closer two dots, the more often they are confused. The colours are the groups the computer found by itself, from the arrows alone and their thickness.

**What it shows.** Four groups, joined by only a few thin arrows, but they are not alike. The red group is one dense knot: every nationality in it is mistaken for every other, and arrows converge on Nigeria and Afghanistan, so the AI talks about all of them in nearly the same way. In the other three groups, the arrows follow clichés or a language instead: Spain, Italy and Brazil (warmth) in amber; the United Kingdom, the United States and Australia (English-speaking) in green; in blue, Belgium and Switzerland around France (French-speaking), Finland and Sweden (reserve), Germany and Japan. France is the big blue dot: answers about Western men that carry no cliché of their own end up there, as a default "Western" answer.

```{=latex}
\end{howtoread}
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5.4
# Gephi-like drawing: stress layout, curved edges coloured by their source, size = arrows received
igraph::V(gnet)$grp <- grp_of[igraph::V(gnet)$name]
igraph::V(gnet)$lab <- nm(igraph::V(gnet)$name)
igraph::V(gnet)$received <- prank[igraph::V(gnet)$name]
r01 <- (igraph::V(gnet)$received - min(prank)) / diff(range(prank))
igraph::V(gnet)$psize <- 2.5 + 8.5 * r01  # dot size
igraph::V(gnet)$tsize <- 2.2 + 1.8 * r01  # label size
igraph::E(gnet)$ecol <- grp_of[igraph::ends(gnet, igraph::E(gnet))[, 1]]
# weighted layout: A -> B and B -> A summed, distance = 1 / rate, so strong confusions are drawn close
unet <- igraph::as_undirected(gnet, mode = "collapse", edge.attr.comb = list(pct = "sum", "ignore"))
set.seed(7)
xy <- graphlayouts::layout_with_stress(unet, weights = 1 / igraph::E(unet)$pct)
ggraph::ggraph(gnet, layout = "manual", x = xy[, 1], y = xy[, 2]) +
  ggraph::geom_edge_arc(aes(colour = ecol, width = pct, alpha = pct), strength = 0.18, lineend = "round",
                        arrow = arrow(length = unit(2.2, "pt"), type = "closed"),
                        end_cap = ggraph::circle(6, "pt")) +
  ggraph::geom_node_point(aes(size = psize, fill = grp), shape = 21, colour = "white", stroke = 0.7) +
  ggraph::geom_node_text(aes(label = lab, colour = grp, size = tsize), family = "Inter",
                         fontface = "bold", repel = TRUE, bg.colour = "white", bg.r = 0.15,
                         point.padding = unit(6, "pt"), box.padding = unit(5, "pt"), force = 3,
                         max.time = 3, seed = 2, show.legend = FALSE) +
  ggraph::scale_edge_colour_manual(values = GRP_COL, guide = "none") +
  ggraph::scale_edge_width(range = c(0.2, 2), guide = "none") +
  ggraph::scale_edge_alpha(range = c(0.25, 0.75), guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = GRP_COL, name = NULL) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = GRP_COL, guide = "none") +
  scale_size_identity() +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 4))) +
  theme_void(base_family = "Inter") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

The classifier's confusions as a network (shared vocabulary, seven models). Arrow A → B: at least 5 % of A's answers guessed as B; width: that share. Dot and label size: PageRank of the nationality in the full matrix of mistakes (where the classifier's errors end up). Colour: Louvain communities computed from the arrows, weighted by their share; an arrow takes the colour of the nationality it leaves. Stress-majorisation layout weighted by the rates (distance = 1 / rate, both directions summed): the more often two nationalities are confused, the closer they are drawn.
:::

::: {#fig-eigen}

```{=latex}
\begin{howtoread}\textbf{How to read this chart}\par\smallskip
```

**Reading.** Each dot is a nationality. Horizontally, the AI judge's verdict (pipeline 1): how much more often the AI says "his origin does not matter" than it pays him a cultural compliment. Vertically, the position of the nationality on the main axis of the classifier's mistakes (pipeline 2), which uses no judge at all. The colours are the groups of the previous chart.

**What it shows.** The two pipelines rank the nationalities in nearly the same order: the dots climb from bottom left (Finland, Japan, Sweden: compliments, and answers easy to tell apart) to top right (Nigeria, Afghanistan: justification, and answers that look alike). Two methods that share nothing but the AI's answers see the same thing.

```{=latex}
\end{howtoread}
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.2
ed <- tibble(country = names(judge_idx), x = judge_idx, y = v2[names(judge_idx)], g = grp_of[names(judge_idx)],
             lab = nm(names(judge_idx)))
ggplot(ed, aes(x, y, colour = g)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = GRID) +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = 1), method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, colour = "#b9b7b1",
              linewidth = 0.4, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(size = 2.2) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = lab), size = 2.6, family = "Inter", seed = 3, show.legend = FALSE,
                           min.segment.length = 0.3, box.padding = 0.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = GRP_COL, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "judge: defensive marking − compliments (points)  →  security guard",
       y = "classifier: 2nd eigenvector of the mistakes") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Two pipelines, one ranking. x: judge index of the TL;DR chart (defensive marking minus positive stereotypes, percentage points, mean of the seven models, LLM judge). y: second eigenvector of the classifier's confusion chain (seven models, no judge), scaled to a maximum of 1 and oriented so that Nigeria is positive. Spearman ρ = `r num(rho_v2, 2)`. Colour: groups of @fig-network.
:::

The second eigenvector agrees with the judge: its Spearman correlation with the index of the TL;DR chart
(defensive marking minus positive stereotypes) is `r num(rho_v2, 2)` (@fig-eigen). The two pipelines share
nothing but the answers: one reads a judged sample, the other every answer of the same seven models.

The classifier's own weights give a second graph (@fig-wordgraph): each nationality is linked to the five
words that point to it most, and a word shared by several nationalities becomes a bridge between them.

::: {#fig-wordgraph}

```{=latex}
\begin{howtoread}\textbf{How to read this chart}\par\smallskip
```

**Reading.** Large dots are nationalities; words in italics are the clues the computer uses to recognise them (in French, as the AI wrote them). A line joins a nationality to one of its five strongest clues; the thicker the line, the stronger the clue. A word with several lines is a clue shared by several nationalities; it is grey when it links nationalities of different groups.

**What it shows.** The biggest hub is *origine* (origin), also the word with the highest PageRank in this graph: it links Albania, Algeria, India, Nigeria and Afghanistan, the men the AI talks about through where they come from. Nigeria is also tied to *argent* (money) and *arnaques* (scams), Afghanistan to *femmes* (women). On the other side, the hubs are compliments: *chaleureux* (warm) for Spain, Italy and Brazil, *ponctualité* for Germany and Switzerland, *humour* for the United Kingdom, Australia and Belgium, and *réservés* (reserved), *discrets* and *silence* for Finland.

```{=latex}
\end{howtoread}
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5.6
LEFTOVER <- c("small", "hope", "need", "gut", "usa")
tt <- read.csv(file.path(GUESS, "top_terms.csv")) |>
  filter(setting == "shared", !grepl(" ", term), !term %in% LEFTOVER) |>
  group_by(country) |> slice_max(coef, n = 5) |> ungroup()
# a word takes the colour of the group of the nationalities it points to, grey when it bridges groups
wgrp <- tt |> mutate(g = grp_of[country]) |> group_by(term) |>
  summarise(g = if (n_distinct(g) == 1) g[1] else "shared")
wn <- bind_rows(tibble(name = unique(tt$country), kind = "nat", g = grp_of[unique(tt$country)]),
                tibble(name = wgrp$term, kind = "word", g = wgrp$g)) |>
  mutate(lab = ifelse(kind == "nat", nm(name), name))
gw <- igraph::graph_from_data_frame(tt |> transmute(from = country, to = term, coef, ecol = grp_of[country]),
                                    vertices = wn)
igraph::V(gw)$deg <- igraph::degree(gw)
# weighted layout: distance = 1 / coefficient, so the strongest clues sit closest to their nationality
set.seed(3)
ggraph::ggraph(gw, layout = "stress", weights = 1 / igraph::E(gw)$coef) +
  ggraph::geom_edge_arc(aes(colour = ecol, width = coef), strength = 0.12, alpha = 0.45, lineend = "round") +
  ggraph::geom_node_point(aes(filter = kind == "nat", fill = g), shape = 21, colour = "white", stroke = 0.7,
                          size = 5.5) +
  ggraph::geom_node_point(aes(filter = kind == "word", colour = g, size = 1 + deg), alpha = 0.35,
                          show.legend = FALSE) +
  # one repel layer for all labels, so that words and nationalities avoid each other
  ggraph::geom_node_text(aes(label = lab, colour = g, size = ifelse(kind == "nat", 3.3, 1.9 + 0.45 * deg),
                             fontface = ifelse(kind == "nat", "bold", "italic")), family = "Inter",
                         repel = TRUE, bg.colour = "white", bg.r = 0.13, seed = 1, show.legend = FALSE,
                         point.padding = unit(2, "pt"), box.padding = unit(1.5, "pt"), min.segment.length = 0.6,
                         segment.colour = "#c9c7c1", segment.size = 0.2, max.overlaps = Inf) +
  scale_size_identity() +
  ggraph::scale_edge_colour_manual(values = GRP_COL, guide = "none") +
  ggraph::scale_edge_width(range = c(0.3, 2.2), guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = GRP_COL, name = NULL) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(GRP_COL, shared = "#6b6a66"), guide = "none") +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 4))) +
  theme_void(base_family = "Inter") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Nationality–clue graph from the classifier's weights (logistic regression on the shared vocabulary of seven models): each nationality is joined to its five single words with the largest positive coefficients; edge width: coefficient. Colours: the communities of @fig-network (not recomputed on this graph); a word takes the colour of the nationalities it points to, grey when it bridges two groups. Stress-majorisation layout weighted by the coefficients (distance = 1 / coefficient). Five leftover words are left out: four English or German words (small, hope, need, gut) and *usa*, which escaped masking.
:::

Lexicometry confirms these words with a statistical test, nationality by nationality (@fig-specificities).

::: {#fig-specificities}

```{=latex}
\begin{howtoread}\textbf{How to read this chart}\par\smallskip
```

**Reading.** Each row is a word, in French as the AI wrote it; each column a nationality. Red means the AI uses this word for this nationality more than chance would explain; blue means it avoids it. The darker the cell, the less likely it is to be chance. Words and nationalities that go together are placed next to each other.

**What it shows.** Two halves. For Western men, Brazilians and Japanese, the over-used words are qualities: *chaleureux* (warm), *ponctualité* (punctuality), *silence*, *humour*. For the others, they are about where the man comes from: *origine*, *ethnique*, *tradition*, *famille*, *religion*, *femme*, and *arnaque* (scam) and *argent* (money) for Nigeria. The blue cells are as telling: *humour*, *silence* and *réservé* (reserved) are almost never used for Turkey, the Maghreb, India, Fiji, Nigeria and Afghanistan. A third family, Brazil, Spain and Italy next to Russia, Romania and Serbia, shares words of language and warmth (*langue*, *traduction*, *chaleureux*).

```{r}
sd_ <- as.data.frame(as.table(as.matrix(sm))) |>
  setNames(c("lemma", "country", "spec")) |>
  mutate(lemma = factor(lemma, rev(rownames(sm))), country = factor(country, colnames(sm)),

ggplot(sd_, aes(country, lemma, fill = spec)) +

  scale_x_discrete(labels = \(x) nm(x), position = "top") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), panel.grid.major = element_blank(), axis.ticks.length = unit(0, "pt"),

        axis.text.x.top = element_text(angle = 50, hjust = 0, vjust = 0),
        axis.text.y = element_text(face = "italic", size = 7),
```

Lafon specificities of the three most over-used lemmas of each nationality (shared vocabulary, all answers of seven models). Cell: signed $-\log_{10} p$ of the hypergeometric test, red for over-use and blue for under-use, clipped at ±10. Rows and columns are ordered by average-linkage clustering.
:::

The Reinert classification finds eight themes in the answers without knowing the nationality, among them
small talk and politeness, culture, emergency calls, physical self-protection, taxi and identity checks,
violence and support helplines. Their shares differ by nationality in the same direction. For Nigeria, the
AI talks less about culture (`r pc(rv("Nigeria", 3))` of the segments, against `r pc(rmean[3])` on average)
and polite conversation (`r pc(rv("Nigeria", 1))` against `r pc(rmean[1])`), and more about emergency calls
(`r pc(rv("Nigeria", 2))` against `r pc(rmean[2])`) and checking the taxi, the name and the identity card
(`r pc(rv("Nigeria", 6))` against `r pc(rmean[6])`). Afghanistan has the same profile without the taxi checks,
and twice as much about violence and support helplines (`r pc(rv("Afghanistan", 7), 1)`, against
`r pc(rv("Finland", 7), 1)` for Finland and `r pc(rv("Japan", 7), 1)` for Japan). The full charts and tables are
in the notebook [@kaggle_guess].

## The worst answers

```{r}
#| label: worst-setup
source("R/worst.R")
W <- score_answers(N)
```

Rates hide what the biased answers actually say. This section quotes the most biased answers of each model,
ranked by severity: an association between the man's origin and a risk (the judge's strongest flag) first,
then a negative stereotype, then a defensive marking ("his origin does not matter"); the alarm score breaks
ties. An answer is kept only if the passage behind its flag is found in the text, and that passage is shown
in **bold** at the centre of the excerpt. Answers flagged only for a high alarm are left out, since caution can
be legitimate. Each excerpt is given in the original French, followed by my English translation. **These are model
outputs, not claims.** The same ranking applied context by context, with three answers per model in each
of the eleven contexts, is given in the appendix.

```{r}
#| label: worst-top
#| results: asis
for (m in names(MODELS)) {
  cat("\n\n### ", LAB[[m]], " {.unnumbered}\n\n", sep = "")
  top <- pick_varied(W |> filter(model == m), 3)
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(top))) cat(entry_md(top[i, ], translate = TRUE))
}
```

The worst answers of the three Gemma models and of Nemotron are mild: their few associations are generic
warnings about romance scams, and the other excerpts only say that the man's origin does not matter. Gemma
E2B's refusals do not appear here, since a refusal quotes nothing; they are the subject of @sec-refusals.
Ministral's are the most explicit of the seven models: it attributes scams and trafficking to Albanian and
Nigerian men, and recalls a "media reputation" of violence for Serbian men before adding that most of them
are ordinary citizens.

# Discussion

**One shared bias, four registers.** The seven models agree on who deserves a compliment: Northern
Europeans, Japanese, Italians and Australians get cultural praise and ice-breakers, Afghans, Nigerians,
Algerians, Russians and Indians rarely. This is the most robust signal of the study, shared by five labs
and by every model size tested. What the models do for the other nationalities differs. Granite, Qwen,
Gemma 26B and Nemotron answer with a justification ("his origin does not matter") that presupposes a
suspicion the user never expressed, and they aim it at the same men: probably an effect of alignment, the
model guarding against accusations of racism only for the groups it associates with that risk, which
reveals the association itself. Ministral does not hide the association: it names the risk, in one answer
in ten overall and in four for an Afghan or a Nigerian man. Gemma E4B does neither, and differs from the
others mostly by what it leaves out. Gemma E2B, the smallest, refuses to help, and refuses most for the
same men. A model that seems neutral on one indicator can therefore be biased on another; a benchmark
limited to explicit associations would have rated the three Gemma models almost perfect, and a benchmark
limited to a judge's reading would have missed Gemma E2B's refusals, the strongest nationality effect
found for that model.

**What size and post-training add.** The Gemma family holds the training recipe constant. Its three sizes
keep the same unequal compliments, but the register for the other men changes with size: refusal for
E2B, near silence for E4B, defensive marking for 26B, aimed at the same nationalities as Granite and Qwen.
Nemotron reaches the same register as 26B from E4B, through NVIDIA's post-training alone. The
"his origin does not matter" reflex is therefore not a trace of pre-training data but something a model
acquires, with more capacity or more alignment, and both routes point it at the same men. A larger model
also tailors its advice more to the man's origin: its nationality is easier to guess from the masked
answer. Making a model larger did not make it fairer; it changed the form of the bias, from a refusal
the woman can see to a suspicion she may not notice.

**Targeted explicit associations.** Explicit negative associations are not spread at random: they
reproduce specific media stereotypes ("419" fraud for Nigeria, refugees and the treatment of women for
Afghanistan) and appear mostly in the online first-date context, where the model links nationality to the
risk of a scam. The Nigeria · scam signal, observed on Granite and declared before the other runs, is found
again on Qwen and Ministral: it is a confirmatory result.

**Two pipelines, one picture.** The judge-free analysis reaches the same conclusion as the judge, with
no judge, on the same seven models, and on every answer instead of a sample. It also adds a finding
the judge's rubric could not reach: the split of the nationalities into two vocabularies, one of qualities
for Western men, Brazilians and Japanese, one of origin, tradition, religion and protection for the others.
The clustering of the judge's indicators (@fig-clusters) and the classifier's confusions (@fig-confusion)
draw the same line, and both single out Nigeria and Afghanistan. The refusals, counted without a judge
too, are a third reading, and they fall on the same men.

**Relation to the RTS report.** I find the "encounter" versus "distrust" contrast described by RTS. In
most of the models tested it is attenuated: these open models rarely tip into outright alarm for a given
nationality, and the bias becomes visible only with a repeated design and a control. Ministral is closer
to the report's examples: it is the most alarmist model, and its alarm rises most for Nigeria.

# Limitations {#sec-limitations}

- **Seven open models, one of them quantised.** Six have 2 to 9 billion parameters (counting the
  effective size of E2B and E4B); Gemma 26B-A4B is a mixture of experts with 4 billion active parameters,
  run in 4-bit AWQ, so its answers are those of the quantised model, which may differ slightly from the
  original. All run on two T4 GPUs; Llama and dense models above 10 billion parameters remain to be done
  (Gemma 4 31B does not fit). One family (Gemma) and one base model / post-training pair (Gemma E4B,
  Nemotron) are too few to generalise what size and post-training do.
- **Refusals are counted by a rule.** The refusal rule (a short answer that opens by declining) was
  checked by reading the answers of every model, but a refusal phrased otherwise would be missed. The
  judge also rates refusals, as neutral answers: they lower Gemma E2B's rates of every indicator without
  being a sign of fairness.
- **The judge is less reliable on some models.** On Ministral, the judge's defensive marking disagrees
  with the bench's regular expression (`r pc(by_model(rx_nat, MI, "judge"))` against
  `r pc(by_model(rx_nat, MI, "regex"))`, rank correlation `r num(rx_rho[[MI]], 2)` over nationalities), and
  part of its negative associations are generic warnings. These two indicators are read with care for
  Ministral; the other models show no such gap.
- **Leftovers in the judge-free pipeline.** A few words in the shared vocabulary still point to a place or a
  language rather than to a stereotype (*Canada*, *SAMU*, *gendarmerie*); they are visible in
  the notebook and must not be read as bias. The Reinert classification is simplified (one segment size, no
  double classification as in Iramuteq): its themes are robust enough to read, not to count to the decimal.
- **The judge is a language model.** Qwen3-32B-AWQ can be wrong, and it belongs to the same family as
  Qwen3.5-9B (self-preference cannot be ruled out). The rubric has not been validated against a
  human-annotated sample; reading the quotes shows false positives (for instance a sentence reassuring the
  user about refugee taxi drivers labelled as a "migration" association). The `asks_clarification` field
  remains poorly calibrated for Granite (about 70 % of answers), probably because of offers at the end of
  answers; it is not used in the analysis.
- **Sample size.** About 99 judged answers per nationality and model: gaps of 2 to 3 points are noise,
  and analyses by context (about 9 verdicts per cell and model) are exploratory.
- **Imperfect masking.** Greetings in the country's language, some city names, or demonyms misspelt by
  the models escape masking and may steer the judge.
- **Protocol.** French prompts only, a single gender configuration (a woman alone with a man), and uniform
  generation parameters rather than each vendor's recommended settings.

# Conclusion

On a controlled design of 7,425 prompts per model, the nationality of a man significantly changes the
safety advice that seven open language models, from five labs, give to a woman alone with him, holding
context and age constant. All seven flatter the same nationalities, Northern Europeans, Japanese and
Italians, and rarely Afghans or Nigerians. For the latter, each model has its own register: defensive
justification (Granite, Qwen, Gemma 26B, Nemotron), explicit associations with scams, migration or the
treatment of women (Ministral, in up to four answers in ten), silence (Gemma E4B), or a refusal to help
(Gemma E2B, up to every request at his place at night for some nationalities). Within the Gemma family,
the defensive reflex comes with size, as it comes with NVIDIA's post-training of Gemma E4B, while the
unequal compliments stay. A second pipeline with no judge finds the same split on the seven models: the
nationality can be guessed from the masked answer six times more often than by chance. Next steps are to
test Llama and larger dense models, to validate the rubric and the refusal rule on a hand-annotated
sample, and to extend the protocol to other languages.
